clue.text: Nothing between boy and girl but a love of wisdom

blocks.note: Phil is a boy's name
nothing is zero, shaped like the letter O
Sophy is an old-fashioned girl's name

explanation.surface: Something romantic comes between a boy and a girl, though it turns out to be only a love of learning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Love' tempts you to read romance, but the love is part of the definition, and 'Nothing' is the letter sitting between the two names.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek roots mean exactly fondness for wisdom, which is how the academic discipline got its name.

clue.text: Astronomer presents orchestra to young leader

indicators.note: the leader of a word is the letter that goes in front, its very first

blocks.note: the Hallé is a famous Manchester orchestra
first letter of young

explanation.surface: A stargazer introduces an orchestra to a promising young conductor.
explanation.walkthrough: The Hallé is Manchester's symphony orchestra; adding the young leader gives HALLEY.
explanation.definitionFit: Edmond Halley was the English astronomer who predicted the return of the comet named after him.

clue.text: Sculptor with some pride in his work?

definitions.text: Sculptor with some pride in his work?

blocks.clueFragment: Sculptor with some pride in his work?
blocks.note: surface reading: an artist who feels proud of what he has made
setter's reading: a pride is a group of lions, which this sculptor made

explanation.surface: An artist who takes a little pride in his craft.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Edwin Landseer sculpted the four bronze lions round Nelson's Column in Trafalgar Square, London: literally a pride in his work.
explanation.definitionFit: Landseer, the Victorian painter, also modelled the famous lion statues, so a group of lions forms part of his output.

clue.text: Laura isn't a type to be involved in an orgy

indicators.note: letters that get involved are mixed up and tangled together, so the words before are rearranged

blocks.note: the letters as written, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: Laura is not the sort of woman to join in wild revelry.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman winter festival of Saturn was famous for licence, so the word now means any riotous revel or debauch.

clue.text: Card game we've come across ?

blocks.note: first meaning: the card game also called twenty-one or blackjack
second meaning: a floating bridge, something we walk across

explanation.surface: A card game we happen to have encountered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Come across' reads as 'happened upon', but it means crossed, literally: a pontoon is a floating bridge.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both the gambling card game played to twenty-one and a temporary floating bridge built on boats or floats.

clue.text: The thread of a story

blocks.note: first meaning: spun fibre used for knitting or weaving
second meaning: a long rambling tale

explanation.surface: The plot line running through a tale.
explanation.definitionFit: The same short word means spun fibre for knitting and also a tall tale, from sailors spinning stories while making rope.

clue.text: Spanish  port-sour blend, but strong

indicators.note: a blend mixes its ingredients together, so the word before is mixed up

blocks.note: Vigo is a port in north-west Spain
rearranged

explanation.surface: A Spanish port wine with a sour edge, but powerful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Port' looks like the fortified wine, but it is a harbour town.
explanation.definitionFit: Vigorous describes something forceful and robust, full of energy, a close synonym of powerful or strong.

clue.text: Placed between editor's pen amendments

indicators.note: amendments are alterations to a text, so the letters before are altered in order

blocks.note: the letters as written, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: Corrections inserted into the text by an editor's pen.
explanation.definitionFit: To interpose is to put something in between two other things, so the past participle matches set in the middle.

clue.text: Bill gets into new suit

indicators.note: something made new is remade in a different form, so the word before is rearranged

blocks.note: AC is short for account, a bill
rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone called Bill puts on a new suit of clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gets into' reads as dressing, but 'into' is the anagram fodder and the suit is a lawsuit.
explanation.definitionFit: A legal action is a lawsuit, a case brought before a court, so both words name the same proceeding.

clue.text: After last walk at sea, heavyweight provides food for the fishes

blocks.note: pirates made victims walk the plank, their final stroll at sea
a ton is a very heavy weight

explanation.surface: A pirate's victim walks the plank, and the heavy body ends up feeding the fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' sets the walk first and the heavyweight second.
explanation.definitionFit: Plankton, the drifting tiny organisms in the sea, are the basic diet of many fish and whales.

clue.text: Poet lent materials for camping centre

indicators.note: the words are raw materials to be worked into something new, so their letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the letters as written

explanation.surface: A poet lends out supplies for a campsite.
explanation.definitionFit: The upright pole stands in the middle of a tent and holds it up, so it is the central support of a camping shelter.

clue.text: Sounds a skinny Stevenson character

indicators.note: sounds says we need what is heard, not the spelling of the following words

blocks.note: a hide is an animal skin; skinny playfully means skin-like

explanation.surface: A thin character from a Robert Louis Stevenson story makes a noise.
explanation.walkthrough: Mr Hyde is the evil side of Dr Jekyll in Stevenson's novella; the setter stretches 'skin' to 'skinny' for the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Edward Hyde is the monstrous alter ego in Stevenson's Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde.

clue.text: Apt to be entertaining?

blocks.note: surface reading: likely to be amusing or fun
setter's reading: inclined to entertain guests at home

explanation.surface: Something that is likely to prove amusing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Entertaining' reads as amusing, but it means having people round as guests.
explanation.definitionFit: A hospitable person is generous and welcoming to visitors, always ready to receive them and give them food and drink.

clue.text: Fools love to get up, of course!

blocks.note: a noodle is a simpleton
love is nil in tennis, shaped like O
taken as written

explanation.surface: Silly people love getting out of bed, naturally!
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of course' looks like 'naturally', but it means something served as a course of a meal.
explanation.definitionFit: A bowl of broth with pasta strands is one dish of a meal, so it is literally part of a course.

clue.text: Does he hang out French articles to dry on the island?

blocks.note: la and un are French words for 'the' and 'a'
taken as written
the Isle of Man, in the Irish Sea

explanation.surface: Does a man hang French goods out to dry on an island?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Articles' suggests clothing, but it means grammatical articles: LA and UN, then DRY, then MAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A man who works in a laundry washes clothes and hangs them out on the line, so the question describes his job.

clue.text: Shock returned  deserters, getting let loose

indicators.note: something returned comes back the way it went, so the following word is read backwards
letters let loose are freed from their order and scattered

blocks.note: rats desert a sinking ship
rearranged

explanation.surface: Deserters coming home and being set free causes a stir.
explanation.definitionFit: To startle someone is to give them a sudden fright or surprise, so the verbs mean the same.

clue.text: Able to come round at four, in this case

indicators.note: coming round something means encircling it, so the first word wraps the others

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
Roman numeral for four

explanation.surface: Able to call round at four o'clock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Case' looks like an event or a box, but it is a grammatical case, and 'four' is a Roman numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: The ablative is a grammatical case in Latin, so a word in this form is in that particular case.

clue.text: Artists find its replacement in some litter

indicators.note: a replacement puts things in different places, so the letters of the word are rearranged
in says the reworked letters go inside the following word

blocks.note: rearranged
a litter of young animals, such as bear cubs

explanation.surface: Painters discover where to replace something among some rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Litter' looks like rubbish; it is a litter of young animals.
explanation.definitionFit: Cubists such as Picasso and Braque were painters of the early twentieth-century movement, so they are artists.

clue.text: Begs Pim to change roles, possibly

indicators.note: to change something is to alter it, so the letters given are put in a new order

blocks.note: the letters as written
the letters as written

explanation.surface: Someone pleads with Pim to swap parts in a play.
explanation.definitionFit: To implore someone is to beseech or plead with them earnestly, a stronger synonym for asking urgently.

clue.text: Girl supplies spanner and tin-opener

indicators.note: the opener of a word is its first letter, the one that begins it

blocks.note: a bridge spans a gap
first letter of tin

explanation.surface: A girl hands over a spanner and a tin-opener from the toolbox.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spanner' looks like the tool, but it is something that spans, and 'tin-opener' is the first letter of tin.
explanation.definitionFit: Bridget is a common female first name, so it is an example of a girl in crossword terms.

clue.text: Unfortunate complaints made by free-trader

indicators.note: letters set free are released from their order and recombined

blocks.note: ills are ailments
rearranged

explanation.surface: Grumbles raised by a merchant who supports free trade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Free-trader' reads as one word, but 'free' is the anagram signal and 'complaints' means illnesses.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone ill-starred was born under an unlucky star, so the word means doomed or luckless.

clue.text: Russia's weighty measure to back party work

indicators.note: going back means travelling the other way, so the words that follow are read backwards

blocks.note: a do is a party
op is short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: Russia's important policy of backing party labour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Weighty measure' sounds like a serious policy, but it is a unit of weight; DO and OP run backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The pood was an old Russian unit of weight, about sixteen kilograms, so it is a measure of heaviness.

clue.text: Infallible guide in gold lace manufacture

indicators.note: manufacture means making something new out of raw materials, so the word before is reshaped

blocks.note: or is gold in heraldry
rearranged

explanation.surface: A sure pointer to quality in the making of gold lace.
explanation.definitionFit: An oracle is a source of supposedly unerring wisdom or prophecy, like the priestess at Delphi.

clue.text: Was there some previous change in date, possibly ?

blocks.clueFragment: Was there some previous change in date, possibly ?
blocks.note: surface reading: a question asking whether a date was moved earlier
setter's reading: a statement meaning was present

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether an appointment was rescheduled.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark turns 'Was there' from a question into a statement about being present at a date that went ahead.
explanation.definitionFit: To have attended an event is to have been present at it, so the past-tense verb matches being there.

clue.text: In a word, a table of facts supplied

indicators.note: in says the letters wanted sit inside the run of words that follows

blocks.note: found spanning the end of word, a, and the start of table

explanation.surface: Put briefly, a table sets out the information provided.
explanation.definitionFit: Data are pieces of information given to work from, a plural noun matching the plural of given facts.

clue.text: Worthless fighter aircraft returned with report

indicators.note: something returned goes back where it came from, so the plane's name is read backwards

blocks.note: the MiG is a Russian fighter plane
a crack is a sharp bang

explanation.surface: A useless warplane came back with an incident report.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Report' looks like a written account, but it is a loud noise such as a gunshot.
explanation.definitionFit: Gimcrack describes something showy but cheaply made and flimsy, so it is a fair synonym for of little value.

clue.text: Abscond to the East Mediterranean

blocks.note: first meaning: an old British slang verb for running off without paying debts
second meaning: the region of the eastern Mediterranean shores

explanation.surface: Someone runs away to the eastern Mediterranean.
explanation.walkthrough: The Levant is the old name for the lands along the eastern Mediterranean coast; to levant is dated British slang for bolting from debts.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both an old slang verb for fleeing creditors and the name for the coastal region from Turkey to Egypt.

clue.text: Amazed by a Pole breaking into an outbuilding

indicators.note: breaking something smashes it apart, so the word that follows is rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
S is the south pole
rearranged
a shed is a small outbuilding

explanation.surface: Surprised by a Polish burglar breaking into a garden shed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Breaking into' reads as burglary, but 'breaking' is the anagram signal for 'into', and the Pole is a compass point.
explanation.definitionFit: Astonished means greatly surprised, a close synonym of struck with wonder or taken aback.
